question.text: Which part of road safety is fully within your control?

answer.text: Other drivers and road conditions are outside your control, but keeping your own vehicle and its tires properly maintained is not.

teaching.text: You cannot control other drivers or the road, but keeping your own vehicle and tires in good shape is entirely up to you. Remember: Your own tires, your job.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Other drivers and road conditions are outside your control, but keeping your own vehicle and its tires properly maintained is not.

question.text: Why do neglected tires matter for safety?

answer.text: Crashes caused by neglected tires are preventable, and running on tires that are under-inflated, over-inflated or low on tread creates safety problems.

teaching.text: Tire-related crashes are preventable, and tires that are under-inflated, over-inflated or worn create real safety problems. Remember: Bad tires, preventable crashes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Crashes caused by neglected tires are preventable, and running on tires that are under-inflated, over-inflated or low on tread creates safety problems.

question.text: How often should you check tire pressure, and with what tool?

answer.text: Check your tire pressure every month using a tire pressure gauge, buying one if you do not already own one.

teaching.text: Once a month, check every tire with a pressure gauge. The target number is printed on a sticker inside the doorframe, and it is measured in pounds per square inch. Remember: Monthly gauge check.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Check your tire pressure every month using a tire pressure gauge, buying one if you do not already own one.

question.text: How do you take an accurate tire pressure reading?

answer.text: To take a reading, remove the cap from the valve stem and press the gauge evenly onto it, and measure while the tires are still cold.

teaching.text: Take the cap off the valve stem, press the gauge on evenly, and measure while the tires are still cold for an accurate reading. Remember: Cap off, gauge on, tires cold.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To take a reading, remove the cap from the valve stem and press the gauge evenly onto it, and measure while the tires are still cold.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Cap off, gauge on, tires cold

question.text: What do you do when the gauge reads above or below the doorframe number?

answer.text: When the gauge shows more pressure than the doorframe number you release air, and when it shows less you add air until the two readings agree.

teaching.text: Compare the gauge with the doorframe number: if it reads higher, let air out; if it reads lower, add air until they match. Remember: Above lets out, below fills.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When the gauge shows more pressure than the doorframe number you release air, and when it shows less you add air until the two readings agree.

question.text: How do you place the penny for the tread test?

answer.text: For the penny tread test, hold a penny by Lincoln's body and push it, Lincoln's head first, into the groove that looks deepest.

teaching.text: For the penny test, hold the coin by Lincoln's body and push it head first into the deepest-looking groove. Remember: Lincoln's head goes in first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For the penny tread test, hold a penny by Lincoln's body and push it, Lincoln's head first, into the groove that looks deepest.

question.text: What does it mean if you can see all of Lincoln's head in the tread?

answer.text: If all of Lincoln's head is visible in the groove, the tread is too worn, so do not drive on those tires and have them replaced.

teaching.text: If you can see Lincoln's whole head, the tread is worn out, so replace those tires. This tread check is a separate inspection from the pressure check with the gauge. Remember: Whole head shows, replace tires.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If all of Lincoln's head is visible in the groove, the tread is too worn, so do not drive on those tires and have them replaced.

question.text: How should you sit in the driver's seat, and why?

answer.text: Sit upright with your back against the seat and your feet on the floor, because slouching can make the vehicle's restraint system less effective.

teaching.text: Sit upright with your back against the seat and feet on the floor, because slouching weakens the restraint system. Remember: Sit up, feet down.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Sit upright with your back against the seat and your feet on the floor, because slouching can make the vehicle's restraint system less effective.

question.text: Why should you adjust your seat and mirrors before starting to drive?

answer.text: Set your seat and mirrors before you start driving so you can see clearly, fully control the pedals and steering wheel, and leave room for an air bag to deploy.

teaching.text: Set the seat and mirrors before you drive so you can see, reach the pedals and wheel, and leave room for the air bag. Remember: Set up before you start.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Set your seat and mirrors before you start driving so you can see clearly, fully control the pedals and steering wheel, and leave room for an air bag to deploy.

question.text: How should your foot move between the pedals in a correct seat position?

answer.text: In a correct seat position your foot pivots smoothly from the brake to the accelerator while your heel stays on the floor.

teaching.text: In a good seat position, your foot pivots between brake and accelerator while your heel stays on the floor. Remember: Heel down, foot pivots.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a correct seat position your foot pivots smoothly from the brake to the accelerator while your heel stays on the floor.

question.text: How high should the top of the steering wheel be?

answer.text: The top of the steering wheel should be no higher than the tops of your shoulders.

teaching.text: Keep the top of the steering wheel at or below the tops of your shoulders. Remember: Wheel top below shoulders.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The top of the steering wheel should be no higher than the tops of your shoulders.

question.text: How much space should be between your chest and the steering wheel?

answer.text: Leave a gap of at least ten inches from your chest to the steering wheel, never move the seat so far forward that steering becomes hard, and do not recline the seat.

teaching.text: Keep at least ten inches between your chest and the wheel, do not crowd the wheel so steering is hard, and do not recline the seat. Remember: Ten inches of air bag room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Leave a gap of at least ten inches from your chest to the steering wheel, never move the seat so far forward that steering becomes hard, and do not recline the seat.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Ten inches of air bag room

question.text: How should you adjust the head restraint?

answer.text: Head restraints are meant to prevent whiplash, so adjust yours to touch the back of your head rather than sit below ear level.

teaching.text: Set the head restraint to touch the back of your head, not below ear level, so it can help prevent whiplash. Remember: Back of head, not neck.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Head restraints are meant to prevent whiplash, so adjust yours to touch the back of your head rather than sit below ear level.

question.text: How does the steering wheel limit differ from the head restraint limit?

answer.text: The steering wheel limit is about height, with its top no higher than your shoulders, while the head restraint limit is about contact, touching the back of your head and not sitting below your ears.

teaching.text: The wheel rule is about height, below your shoulders, while the head restraint rule is about contact with the back of your head. Remember: Wheel height, restraint contact.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The steering wheel limit is about height, with its top no higher than your shoulders, while the head restraint limit is about contact, touching the back of your head and not sitting below your ears.

question.text: Which mirror is your primary view to the rear, and how is it set?

answer.text: The rearview mirror, the interior mirror mounted on the windshield, is your primary mirror for seeing what is behind you.

teaching.text: The interior rearview mirror is your main view behind you. Set it to frame the whole rear window, and switch a day-night mirror to match the time of day. Remember: Rearview mirror leads.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The rearview mirror, the interior mirror mounted on the windshield, is your primary mirror for seeing what is behind you.

question.text: What are outside mirrors adjusted to do?

answer.text: Outside mirrors are set to shrink blind spots, the areas where your view is blocked, and to give the widest possible view to the sides and rear.

teaching.text: Outside mirrors are adjusted to cut down blind spots and give you the widest view to the sides and rear. Remember: Shrink the blind spots.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Outside mirrors are set to shrink blind spots, the areas where your view is blocked, and to give the widest possible view to the sides and rear.

question.text: How do you set the left outside mirror using the enhanced method?

answer.text: For the enhanced left mirror setting, rest your head against the closed window on your left and adjust the mirror until the rear edge of your vehicle barely shows.

teaching.text: For the enhanced left mirror, lean your head against the closed left window and adjust until your car's rear edge barely shows. Remember: Head to window, edge barely.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For the enhanced left mirror setting, rest your head against the closed window on your left and adjust the mirror until the rear edge of your vehicle barely shows.

question.text: How do you set the right outside mirror using the enhanced method?

answer.text: The right outside mirror uses a different method from the left: lean right until your head is under the rearview mirror or over the center console, then adjust until the right edge of your vehicle is just visible.

teaching.text: For the enhanced right mirror, lean right so your head is under the rearview mirror or over the console, then adjust until the right edge just shows. Remember: Lean to center, edge barely.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The right outside mirror uses a different method from the left: lean right until your head is under the rearview mirror or over the center console, then adjust until the right edge of your vehicle is just visible.

question.text: What do enhanced outside mirror settings trade away, and what do they gain?

answer.text: Enhanced outside mirror settings hide your own vehicle's sides when you glance at them, but add twelve to sixteen degrees of extra viewing area on each side.

teaching.text: Enhanced mirror settings hide your own car's sides when you glance, but they add twelve to sixteen degrees of extra view on each side. Remember: Lose your sides, gain view.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Enhanced outside mirror settings hide your own vehicle's sides when you glance at them, but add twelve to sixteen degrees of extra viewing area on each side.

question.text: Who in the vehicle must be using a safety belt or child restraint?

answer.text: Always buckle your own safety belt and make sure every passenger is using a safety belt or a child restraint.

teaching.text: Buckle your own belt and make sure every passenger has a safety belt or child restraint before you move. Remember: Everyone buckled, every trip.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Always buckle your own safety belt and make sure every passenger is using a safety belt or a child restraint.

question.text: How do safety belts protect you in a collision?

answer.text: Studies show safety belts greatly cut your chance of injury or death in a collision, keep you from being thrown from the vehicle and help the driver stay in control.

teaching.text: Safety belts greatly lower the chance of injury or death, keep you inside the vehicle and help you stay in control in a crash. Remember: Belts keep you in control.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Studies show safety belts greatly cut your chance of injury or death in a collision, keep you from being thrown from the vehicle and help the driver stay in control.

question.text: What does South Carolina's primary safety belt law allow an officer to do?

answer.text: South Carolina has a primary safety belt enforcement law, so an officer with a clear and unobstructed view of a driver or occupant who is unbelted, or not in a child restraint, may stop the driver.

teaching.text: South Carolina uses primary enforcement, so an officer who clearly sees an unbelted occupant or an unrestrained child may stop the driver. Remember: Unbuckled is enough to stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: South Carolina has a primary safety belt enforcement law, so an officer with a clear and unobstructed view of a driver or occupant who is unbelted, or not in a child restraint, may stop the driver.

question.text: How should the shoulder harness be worn?

answer.text: Wear the shoulder harness across your shoulder and chest with little or no slack, never under your arm or behind your back, since that can cause serious internal injuries in a collision.

teaching.text: The shoulder harness goes across your shoulder and chest with little slack, never under the arm or behind the back. Remember: Across chest, never behind.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Wear the shoulder harness across your shoulder and chest with little or no slack, never under your arm or behind your back, since that can cause serious internal injuries in a collision.

question.text: How should the lap belt be adjusted?

answer.text: After fastening, adjust the lap belt so it is snug and sits low across your hips, or you could slide out of it in a collision and be hurt or killed.

teaching.text: Pull the lap belt snug and low across your hips so you cannot slide out of it in a collision. Remember: Snug and low on hips.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After fastening, adjust the lap belt so it is snug and sits low across your hips, or you could slide out of it in a collision and be hurt or killed.

question.text: How do the shoulder harness and lap belt positions differ?

answer.text: The shoulder part of the belt goes across the shoulder and chest, while the lap part goes snug and low across the hips, and each misplaced part brings its own collision injury risk.

teaching.text: Two straps, two jobs: the shoulder part crosses the chest and the lap part sits low on the hips, and either one misplaced can injure you. Remember: Chest strap, hip strap.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The shoulder part of the belt goes across the shoulder and chest, while the lap part goes snug and low across the hips, and each misplaced part brings its own collision injury risk.

question.text: Should you wear a safety belt if your vehicle has air bags?

answer.text: Keep wearing safety belts even when your vehicle is equipped with air bags.

teaching.text: Air bags do not replace belts, so keep buckling up even in a vehicle with air bags. Remember: Air bags plus belts.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep wearing safety belts even when your vehicle is equipped with air bags.

question.text: What role do air bags play alongside safety belts?

answer.text: Air bags are supplemental restraints designed to work best together with safety belts, lowering the chance that your head and upper body hit the vehicle's interior.

teaching.text: Air bags are supplemental restraints that work best with belts, keeping your head and upper body from hitting the interior. Remember: Air bags only supplement.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Air bags are supplemental restraints designed to work best together with safety belts, lowering the chance that your head and upper body hit the vehicle's interior.

question.text: How do safety belts help the air bag work?

answer.text: Safety belts put your body in the right position to get the most from the air bag, and your vehicle owner's manual describes the air bags in your vehicle.

teaching.text: A belt holds your body in the right spot for the air bag to help, and the owner's manual explains your vehicle's air bags. Remember: Belts position you right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Safety belts put your body in the right position to get the most from the air bag, and your vehicle owner's manual describes the air bags in your vehicle.

question.text: What two rules apply to child safety seats and air bags?

answer.text: A child safety seat must be installed properly and used correctly, and a rear-facing child seat must never be placed in front of an air bag.

teaching.text: Install and use every child seat correctly, and never place a rear-facing seat in front of an air bag. Remember: Never rear-facing before an air bag.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A child safety seat must be installed properly and used correctly, and a rear-facing child seat must never be placed in front of an air bag.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Never rear-facing before an air bag

question.text: Where must children age seven and younger ride?

answer.text: Children age seven and younger must ride in a car seat in the back seat so an air bag cannot injure them in a collision.

teaching.text: Children seven and younger ride in a car seat in the back seat, out of reach of a deploying air bag. Remember: Seven and under, back seat.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Children age seven and younger must ride in a car seat in the back seat so an air bag cannot injure them in a collision.

question.text: What restraint must an infant under age two use?

answer.text: An infant under age two must be secured in a rear-facing car seat in a rear seat until the child exceeds the seat maker's height or weight limit.

teaching.text: Babies under two ride rear-facing in a rear seat until they exceed the seat maker's height or weight limit. Remember: Under two faces back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: An infant under age two must be secured in a rear-facing car seat in a rear seat until the child exceeds the seat maker's height or weight limit.

question.text: When does a child move to a forward-facing car seat?

answer.text: A child at least age two, or a younger child who has outgrown the rear-facing seat's limits, must ride in a forward-facing car seat in a rear seat until exceeding that seat's height or weight limits.

teaching.text: From age two, or sooner once the rear-facing seat is outgrown, a child rides forward-facing in a rear seat until that seat's limits are reached. Remember: Two or outgrown, face forward.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A child at least age two, or a younger child who has outgrown the rear-facing seat's limits, must ride in a forward-facing car seat in a rear seat until exceeding that seat's height or weight limits.

question.text: Does age alone decide when a child switches from a rear-facing seat?

answer.text: Moving a child from a rear-facing to a forward-facing seat depends on age two or on outgrowing the rear-facing seat's height or weight limit, not on age alone.

teaching.text: Moving to forward-facing depends on reaching age two or outgrowing the rear-facing seat, so size can matter as much as age. Remember: Age or size decides.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Moving a child from a rear-facing to a forward-facing seat depends on age two or on outgrowing the rear-facing seat's height or weight limit, not on age alone.

question.text: When does a child move to a booster seat, and for how long?

answer.text: A child at least age four who has outgrown the forward-facing car seat must use a booster seat in a rear seat until the adult safety belt fits correctly.

teaching.text: From age four, once the forward-facing seat is outgrown, a child rides in a booster in a rear seat until the adult belt fits. Remember: Four and up, booster time.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A child at least age four who has outgrown the forward-facing car seat must use a booster seat in a rear seat until the adult safety belt fits correctly.

question.text: Which belts hold a booster seat in place?

answer.text: A booster seat is held in place by both the lap and the shoulder belt, not by the lap belt alone.

teaching.text: A booster seat needs both the lap belt and the shoulder belt holding it, never the lap belt alone. Remember: Booster needs both belts.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A booster seat is held in place by both the lap and the shoulder belt, not by the lap belt alone.

question.text: When may a child use an adult safety belt?

answer.text: A child at least age eight, or at least fifty-seven inches tall, may use an adult safety belt if that belt can secure the child properly.

teaching.text: At age eight, or once fifty-seven inches tall, a child may use an adult belt as long as it fits properly. Remember: Eight or tall enough.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A child at least age eight, or at least fifty-seven inches tall, may use an adult safety belt if that belt can secure the child properly.

question.text: How do the back seat rule and the adult belt rule differ?

answer.text: The back seat rule covers children age seven and younger in a car seat, while the adult belt rule starts at age eight or a height of fifty-seven inches, so the two rules answer different questions.

teaching.text: The back seat rule tells you where children seven and under sit, while the adult belt rule tells you when a child may switch to a regular belt. Remember: Where to sit versus what restrains.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The back seat rule covers children age seven and younger in a car seat, while the adult belt rule starts at age eight or a height of fifty-seven inches, so the two rules answer different questions.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Where to sit versus what restrains

question.text: Where can you read South Carolina's child passenger safety law?

answer.text: The South Carolina child passenger safety law is SC Code §fifty-six-five-six thousand four hundred ten, and it can be read on the Buckle Up, South Carolina website.

teaching.text: South Carolina's child passenger safety law is in the state code, and you can read it on the Buckle Up, South Carolina website. Remember: Buckle Up, South Carolina.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The South Carolina child passenger safety law is SC Code §fifty-six-five-six thousand four hundred ten, and it can be read on the Buckle Up, South Carolina website.

question.text: What is the penalty for driving with an unsecured load?

answer.text: Driving with an unsecured load is illegal and very dangerous, and a driver who fails to secure one is guilty of a misdemeanor and may pay a fine plus the cost of cleaning up the spilled material.

teaching.text: An unsecured load is illegal and dangerous, and the driver can be charged with a misdemeanor, fined and billed for the cleanup. Remember: Loose load, misdemeanor.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driving with an unsecured load is illegal and very dangerous, and a driver who fails to secure one is guilty of a misdemeanor and may pay a fine plus the cost of cleaning up the spilled material.

question.text: When is a load considered secure?

answer.text: A load is secure only when nothing can slide, shift, fall or sift onto the road or be blown into the air.

teaching.text: A load is only secure when nothing can slide, shift, fall, sift onto the road or blow away. Remember: Nothing slides, falls or flies.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A load is secure only when nothing can slide, shift, fall or sift onto the road or be blown into the air.

question.text: How should you secure a load?

answer.text: Tie a load directly to the vehicle or trailer with rope, netting or straps, and think about covering all of it with a sturdy tarp or netting.

teaching.text: Tie cargo directly to the vehicle or trailer with rope, netting or straps, and consider covering it all with a sturdy tarp or netting. Remember: Tie it down, tarp it.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Tie a load directly to the vehicle or trailer with rope, netting or straps, and think about covering all of it with a sturdy tarp or netting.

question.text: What else does the manual say about loads besides tying them down?

answer.text: Do not overload your vehicle or trailer, double-check every load before leaving, and remember that animals you carry must also be properly secured.

teaching.text: Never overload a vehicle or trailer, double-check every load before you go, and secure any animals you carry. Remember: No overload, animals too.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not overload your vehicle or trailer, double-check every load before leaving, and remember that animals you carry must also be properly secured.

question.text: What should you ask yourself before driving with a load?

answer.text: Before driving with a load, ask whether anything could fall or blow off, whether it is secured at the back, sides and top, how it would react to hard braking, a bump or a crash, and whether you would feel safe driving behind it.

teaching.text: Before you drive off with a load, ask whether anything could come loose and whether you would feel safe driving behind it. Remember: Would you follow it?.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before driving with a load, ask whether anything could fall or blow off, whether it is secured at the back, sides and top, how it would react to hard braking, a bump or a crash, and whether you would feel safe driving behind it.

question.text: What do driver assistance safety features do?

answer.text: Driver assistance safety features in many newer vehicles sense conditions and spot dangers, then either alert you with sounds or vibration or take control by adjusting braking or steering.

teaching.text: Assistance features sense conditions and dangers, then either warn you with sound or vibration or step in on braking or steering. Remember: Sense, then warn or act.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driver assistance safety features in many newer vehicles sense conditions and spot dangers, then either alert you with sounds or vibration or take control by adjusting braking or steering.

question.text: How do warning-only features differ from intervening features?

answer.text: Some assistance features only warn you with sounds or vibration, while others can step in by adjusting the braking or steering.

teaching.text: Some features only alert you, while others can actually adjust the braking or steering. Remember: Some alert, some steer.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Some assistance features only warn you with sounds or vibration, while others can step in by adjusting the braking or steering.

question.text: Which features count as driver assistance features?

answer.text: Features of this kind include blind spot warning, forward collision warning, automatic emergency braking, a backup camera, active parking assist and lane keeping assistance.

teaching.text: Common assistance features include blind spot and forward collision warnings, automatic emergency braking, a backup camera, parking assist and lane keeping. Remember: Warnings, braking, camera, assist.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Features of this kind include blind spot warning, forward collision warning, automatic emergency braking, a backup camera, active parking assist and lane keeping assistance.

question.text: Which features may you not use during the driving test?

answer.text: During your driving test you will not be allowed to use certain features, such as parking assist and cruise control.

teaching.text: On the driving test, some features are off limits, such as parking assist and cruise control. Remember: No parking assist on test.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: During your driving test you will not be allowed to use certain features, such as parking assist and cruise control.

question.text: Which two features does the manual name as off limits on the driving test?

answer.text: Cruise control and parking assist are both named as features you may not use during the driving test, even though parking assist is listed among the safety features.

teaching.text: Parking assist counts as a safety feature, yet it is still banned on the driving test along with cruise control. Remember: Cruise and parking assist off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Cruise control and parking assist are both named as features you may not use during the driving test, even though parking assist is listed among the safety features.

question.text: Do assistance features drive the vehicle for you?

answer.text: Assistance features help with the driving task but do not drive the vehicle for you, so you must stay engaged and focused the whole time.

teaching.text: Assistance features help with driving but never drive for you, so stay engaged and focused the whole time. Remember: They help, you drive.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Assistance features help with the driving task but do not drive the vehicle for you, so you must stay engaged and focused the whole time.

question.text: Who stays responsible for seeing around the vehicle when it has safety features?

answer.text: You stay responsible for seeing everything around you through head checks, mirrors and cameras, and for operating the vehicle safely, so never depend on safety features alone.

teaching.text: You are still responsible for seeing everything around you with head checks, mirrors and cameras, so never rely on features alone. Remember: Head checks still matter.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You stay responsible for seeing everything around you through head checks, mirrors and cameras, and for operating the vehicle safely, so never depend on safety features alone.

question.text: When might assistance features not work properly?

answer.text: Learn from the owner's manual how your safety features work and where they fall short, because they may not work properly in rain, snow, ice, fog, on hills or in curves.

teaching.text: Read the owner's manual to learn your features' limits, because rain, snow, ice, fog, hills and curves can stop them from working properly. Remember: Weather and curves fool sensors.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Learn from the owner's manual how your safety features work and where they fall short, because they may not work properly in rain, snow, ice, fog, on hills or in curves.

question.text: How should you maintain sensors and software for assistance features?

answer.text: Keep vehicle sensors clean and free of damage, and keep the software up to date where it applies, following the vehicle maker's recommendations.

teaching.text: Keep sensors clean and undamaged, and keep the software current where it applies, as the vehicle maker recommends. Remember: Clean sensors, current software.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep vehicle sensors clean and free of damage, and keep the software up to date where it applies, following the vehicle maker's recommendations.

question.text: What can assistance features do when used properly?

answer.text: Used properly, assistance features offer real benefits and could help reduce crashes, injuries and deaths.

teaching.text: Used the right way, assistance features bring real benefits and could help cut crashes, injuries and deaths. Remember: Used right, they help.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Used properly, assistance features offer real benefits and could help reduce crashes, injuries and deaths.

recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of securing a load. An unsecured load is a misdemeanor, and a load is secure only when nothing can slide, shift, fall, sift or blow off. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Assistance features help but never drive for you, and parking assist and cruise control are off limits on the driving test.
